# Devpost submission - ready to paste

*Every number below is regenerated by a command in the repository. Nothing here
is typed twice.*

---

## Project Title

**WIIGA - the water goes where it is needed, when it is needed, on the cleanest
power available**

*Wiiga* means "the well" in Moore, the language spoken in Ouagadougou.

---

## One day, to make the numbers mean something

**25 February. 38.7 C. Hot dry season, when Ouagadougou is thirstiest and the
grid fails every evening.**

That day, the best hand-written rulebook leaves 222 256 litres unserved -
**11 113 people below the WHO survival threshold of 20 litres. Half the city.**

The agent, same day, same outages, same sunshine, same demand: **546 people.**
**A difference of 10 566 people, in one day.**

The five days where that gap is largest are all in the hot dry season, between
38 and 40 C. The agent's value does not spread evenly across the year - it
concentrates exactly on the days the city can least afford.

---

## Problem Statement

In most cities, the water pumps simply run. All of them, most of the day, so
that water is always there. It is the safest thing an operator can do, and in
Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso, it collides with a hard fact: **the electricity grid
is load-shed about eight hours a day, and hardest in the evening** - exactly when
a residential district wants water.

The utility runs a fixed setting written years ago: full power at night, idle by
day. In our simulation it leaves the worst-served district **without water 2.48
hours a day**, burns 77 litres of diesel doing it, and is the most expensive
policy we measured. Three costs, all paid by the same people:

- **Districts run dry**, and averages hide it - a policy that keeps two districts
  full and drains a third looks excellent on a dashboard.
- **Diesel burns to catch up**, the dirtiest and costliest source, used precisely
  when it is least affordable.
- **Nobody is warned.** The cut arrives, the tap is dry, and the household that
  could have filled a jerrycan an hour earlier did not know.

The decision is genuinely hard. To know whether to pump *now*, an operator must
hold four things together that do not arrive at the same time: the district's
peak six hours out, the sun's arc, the risk of a cut this evening, and how much
diesel is left. Nobody does that well by hand, twenty-four times a day, forever.

---

## Solution Overview

WIIGA builds a **digital twin** of the water network - three district tanks,
three pumps, three energy sources, a grid that fails, demand that follows heat
and holidays - calibrated on three years of measured daily records for
Ouagadougou. A PPO agent then operates that twin, deciding every hour **which
pump runs, at what power, filling which tank, on which energy source.**

Three moments from one simulated day, all replayable in the live demo:

**1 p.m. - it fills the tanks on sunlight it does not pay for.** All three pumps
at 100 %, all three on solar. Nobody is thirsty at 1 p.m.; the agent is not
serving demand, it is **storing work already done**. Storing that solar energy
would normally mean lithium batteries. The storage is already on site: it is the
tank.

**7 p.m. - peak demand, grid down, sun gone, and it barely pumps.** Pumps at
0 %, 7 %, 0 %. It does not need to - the worst district is at 57 % and nobody
goes dry. It did not react to the evening. It prepared for it at midday.

**3 a.m. - it hands the station back to the operator.** The agent has an action
meaning *not this hour, you take it*, and it pays 3.0 of reward every time it
uses it. At night there is no sun to trade, no peak to anticipate, no outage to
fear, and the old fixed setting is simply the right answer. **The agent learned
when it is useless**, and steps aside. For a utility, that is the opposite of
what they fear from software like this.

Two design decisions separate this from published pump scheduling:

**The reward reads the worst-served district, not the average.** `min`, not
`mean`. With an average, draining one district to keep two full is a good policy.

**The agent can talk to the city.** See below - it is the part with no equivalent
we could find.

---

## Key Features

### 1. It decides when to warn the city

One action touches no pump: **broadcast a warning to fill jerrycans before the
cut**. This does not exist in the pump-scheduling literature for a reason that is
not technical - **in Europe nobody stores water at home.** Published demand
response shifts *industrial* load through *pricing*. Here every household has
containers, and one sentence at 5 p.m. moves more water than an hour of diesel.

It is not a free button. **Credibility is a depletable resource**: a correct
warning buys +0.04 of the city's trust, a false one costs -0.15. That asymmetry
alone fixes a break-even accuracy of **78.9 %**, and no penalty term forbids
chatter - it is simply a losing bet the agent has to work out.

Measured over a year: **0.70 warnings a day, right 96 % of the time**, with
trust climbing to its maximum. And the other half of the number, because
precision alone flatters: it warns before **173 of 641 outages**, so 27 % recall.
That is the operating point the credibility economy forces - buy precision, give
up coverage, because an agent believed by nobody helps nobody.

**The speech is not decoration.** Same weights, warning switched off: **45 % more
dry hours and 8 % more expensive**.

### 2. It knows what time of year it is

Ouagadougou has three water problems, not one. April: 39.8 C, demand up a
quarter, grid failing every evening - but clear skies, so the tank-as-battery
works. August: 30.1 C and 8.7 mm of rain a day - demand falls, and so does the
sunshine the battery depends on. The two seasons want opposite policies, which is
why no fixed setting holds both. Tabaski multiplies a day's demand by 1.6 on
tanks that do not grow for the occasion.

### 3. It works in a city it has never seen

Type a city name: geocoding and three years of daily records arrive in about two
seconds, no API key, no account, cached to disk so the demo runs offline.

Then the honest test - Ouagadougou weights, replayed unchanged: it beats the
rulebook in **3 of 5 cities** and loses in 2. We publish that, because the
pattern is worth more than a clean sweep: **its advantage tracks how hard the
city is.** Where a rulebook already keeps taps running, there is nothing to win.

### 4. It says how much infrastructure it replaces

Because the twin models the real network, it answers capital questions. The
rulebook only matches the agent at **1.22x storage - 96 m3 of new tank on the 440
that exist.** That is what the agent is worth in concrete, and it costs nothing
to pour.

### 5. Every number regenerates from a command

Two scripts produce JSON; the README and the web page read them. If a figure is
wrong, the measurement is wrong, and it is fixed at the source.

## Technologies Used

| | |
|---|---|
| **Reinforcement learning** | Stable-Baselines3 2.7.1 (PPO), Gymnasium 1.2.3 |
| **Numerics** | NumPy |
| **Data** | Open-Meteo geocoding + ERA5 daily archive, keyless, 2023-2025 |
| **Demo** | one static HTML file with its data written inside it - no server, no serverless function, no network request |
| **Language** | Python 3.13 |

Deliberately absent: no LLM, no cloud API, no GPU. Training takes about ten
minutes on a laptop CPU across 8 parallel environments, and the whole project
runs offline. **A utility in Ouagadougou can run this on the hardware it has.**

---

## Target Users

**Directly: the operators of a small urban water utility** in a city with an
unreliable grid - Ouagadougou, Bobo-Dioulasso, and the several hundred cities
across the Sahel and South Asia under the same constraint. The agent produces an
hourly schedule, and because it can hand any hour back, it can be adopted
gradually rather than trusted all at once.

**Through them: the 22 000 people** in the three modelled districts. The unit
that matters is not cubic metres, it is **person-days above the WHO survival
threshold of 20 litres**: WIIGA keeps **148 455 person-days a year** above it
compared to the best hand-written rulebook, and **1 004 745** compared to what
the utility runs today.

**And whoever plans the network**, who can ask the twin how much storage is
needed before anyone pours concrete.

---

## Results

| | agent | best rulebook | current practice |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| dry hours / day | **0.16** | 0.33 | 2.48 |
| people below WHO survival / day | **113** | 520 | 1 887 |
| kg CO2 / day | **107** | 168 | 206 |
| cost / day (FCFA) | **268 745** | 321 557 | 961 761 |

**53 % fewer dry hours than the best hand-written rulebook**, which reads the
same outage forecast the agent does. **48 % less CO2 than current practice**,
22 tonnes a year.

**And it survives being attacked.** PPO is stochastic, so we trained three seeds:
all three beat the rulebook, by 54 % on average and 37-72 % depending on the
seed. The rulebook's own constants were swept over a 6x5 grid - ours was
under-tuned by 13 %, and the agent still beats **the best of the family by 62 %**.
The hand-set constants were swept from 23 to 366 litres of diesel a day. Fifteen
property tests run in one command with no dependencies. And a module exists whose
only job is to attack our main claim: the agent gains 18 % of reward and 59 % of
task performance, a ratio of 0.31 - a reward hacker scores the opposite.

---

## What did not work

Six mechanisms were built, measured, and thrown away. Each is documented in the
code at the exact line where it failed, because a project that reports only its
successes is a project you cannot check.

- **Trust clamped at zero made lying free.** Once at the floor the subtraction was
  clipped, so a false alarm cost nothing while household response was already
  zero. The agent fell into that absorbing state and stayed, broadcasting seven
  times a day at 57 % accuracy. Below zero there is not an absence of trust but
  *active disbelief*.
- **Letting the agent repeat itself produced two opposite degenerate optima.**
  Same reward, two seeds: one never spoke at all, the other shouted seven times a
  day and hit the distrust floor on day 14 *despite 87 % accuracy*. The fix is
  what every real alerting system does - the broadcaster does not re-send while
  the previous warning is still awaiting judgement.
- **The textbook form of potential-based reward shaping charged rent.**
  `gamma * Phi(s') - Phi(s)` costs `(1-gamma) * Phi` every step merely for
  *holding* the potential: a day with no warning at all cost -10.6, and a trusted
  utility paid twice what a discredited one paid. It rewarded destroying your own
  reputation.
- **Raising the discount factor to see reputation further ahead broke the
  pumping.** At 0.995 all three seeds fell *below* the rulebook. The two
  sub-problems do not share a natural horizon: pumping is intraday, the tanks
  refill every morning.
- **Ending the episode at midnight told the agent the future was worthless.**
  Harmless while only tanks existed - they refill - but reputation crosses days.
  Midnight is a measurement boundary, not the end of the world.
- **Our own baseline was a straw man.** The "current practice" policy never
  started its generator: it pumped on the grid through the outage, scoring 0.0
  litres of diesel a day - a perfect carbon footprint achieved by serving nobody -
  and made the agent look ten times better than it is. Corrected, and the CO2
  comparison became worth making.

---

## What we are not claiming

- **PPO is from 2017**, potential-based reward shaping from 1999, max-min
  fairness is a classic. **Nothing in the method is new.** What is new is the
  objective and the communication action.
- **Everything here is simulated.** These are claims about a digital twin
  calibrated on measured climatology, not measurements taken in Ouagadougou.
- **The load-shedding model is hand-calibrated.** No utility publishes outage
  records. The agent's advantage is measured against rules living under the
  *same* model, so the comparison stays fair even where the model is wrong.
- **Transfer between cities is climatic only.** District profiles, tank sizes and
  the load-shedding regime stay those of Ouagadougou.
- **Household response to a warning is a model, not a survey.**
- **There is a budget above which this stops being useful.** At 366 litres of
  diesel a day the rulebook wins, because the generator then covers more than
  half the city's pumping energy and there is no arbitrage left to make. WIIGA is
  for utilities that are constrained.
